title: Critics and Conversations
bigQuestion: Which of Heiser's ideas do most scholars share, which are debated, and how can a reader weigh an argument fairly?

story.title: Two Stacks of Books
story.kicker: Two seminary students read the same psalm and reach different conclusions, and neither will let the other off easy.
paragraphs: It is late on a weekday evening in a seminary library. Two students, Dana and Marcus, share a long table near the reference shelves. Each has a stack of commentaries on the Psalms. Between them lies an open Hebrew Bible, turned to Psalm 82. They are writing a joint paper for a class on the Psalms, and they cannot agree on the first sentence.

Dana has been reading Michael Heiser's The Unseen Realm. She taps the first verse. God stands in the council of El, she says, and judges among the gods. The same kind of phrase shows up at Ugarit for an assembly of divine beings. And verse 7 says they will die like humans. You only say that to someone who is not human.

Marcus opens an older commentary. It reads the gods as judges in Israel, who ruled in God's name and were called gods because of their office. He points to John 10:34, where Jesus quotes the psalm while arguing with people in Jerusalem. He says some interpreters read Jesus as speaking about human leaders there. Then he slides over a third book that reads the psalm as addressed to Israel at Mount Sinai.

Dana writes three words across the top of a notepad: claim, evidence, counter-evidence. Under claim she writes her reading and his. Under evidence each of them lists verses and parallels. Under counter-evidence each has to write the strongest point against their own view. Marcus groans, then laughs, and starts writing.

By closing time their paper still has two readings, but now each is stated fairly. They have also learned something about scholarship. Some points in this debate are widely agreed, some are still argued, and good readers know which is which. This chapter maps that ground.
story.think: Why might writing the strongest point against your own view make your paper better?

lessons.title: The Council in Scholarship
lessons.mainIdea: The idea that the Hebrew Bible pictures a divine council was well established in scholarship before Heiser, in works such as E. Theodore Mullen's 1980 study.
reading: Heiser did not invent the divine council. Scholars had discussed it for decades before The Unseen Realm (2015). Frank Moore Cross wrote about it in Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic (1973). E. Theodore Mullen devoted a whole book to it: The Assembly of the Gods: The Divine Council in Canaanite and Early Hebrew Literature (1980). Mark S. Smith discussed it in The Early History of God (1990) and later works.

These scholars pointed to council scenes across the Hebrew Bible. In 1 Kings 22:19–22 the prophet Micaiah describes the LORD on his throne with the host of heaven around him, discussing a plan. Job 1–2 opens in a heavenly court. Isaiah 6 shows the prophet in God's throne room asking, whom shall I send, and who will go for us? And Psalm 82 names the council outright.

So when Heiser wrote about the council, he was building on a broad base. Most scholars accept that the texts use council imagery. What they debate is how to explain it. Some, like Smith, see it as a leftover from Israel's Canaanite past that faded over time. Heiser saw it as a steady part of the Bible's worldview from start to finish.

Heiser's own contribution was to trace the idea across the whole Bible for a wide audience. He wrote his dissertation on the council in Second Temple texts (2004), then wrote popular books. He linked the council to many other topics: Eden, Genesis 6, the nations, and the New Testament.

words.d: a biblical phrase for the heavenly beings around God's throne; sometimes used for the stars
the place of a king's court; in the Bible, the setting of several heavenly council scenes
broad agreement among most experts in a field

look.prompt: What details in this verse make it look like a royal court? Why would scholars call it a council scene?

check.q: Who wrote The Assembly of the Gods (1980)?
check.why: E. Theodore Mullen published The Assembly of the Gods, a study of the divine council, in 1980.

check.why: 1 Kings 22:19–22 records Micaiah's vision of the heavenly court.

lessons.title: Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Scrolls
lessons.mainIdea: A Dead Sea Scroll reads sons of God in Deuteronomy 32:8 where the later Masoretic Text reads sons of Israel, and most text critics prefer the scroll's reading.
reading: Deuteronomy 32 is the Song of Moses. Verse 8 describes the Most High dividing the nations and setting their borders. The *Masoretic Text*, the standard Hebrew text used in most Bibles, ends the verse with according to the number of the sons of Israel. That is the reading behind the King James Version.

In the caves near Qumran, found from 1947 onward, scholars recovered a copy of Deuteronomy known as 4QDeut j. It is centuries older than the oldest complete Masoretic manuscripts. At verse 8 it reads sons of God, bene elohim. The *Septuagint*, the ancient Greek translation, has a reading that points the same way; most of its copies say angels of God. Text critics compare such witnesses to decide which reading is most likely original.

Most text critics now prefer sons of God. Several modern translations, such as the English Standard Version and the New Revised Standard Version, follow it. Heiser argued for this reading in a 2001 article in the journal Bibliotheca Sacra. He made it a key to his whole approach. In his reading, the verse says God placed the nations under members of his council, while Israel remained his own (verse 9).

Text critics call the study of manuscript differences *textual criticism*. The word criticism here does not mean finding fault with the Bible. It means judging carefully between readings. Many scholars who disagree with Heiser's larger framework still accept the scroll's reading of this verse.

words.d: the standard Hebrew text of the Hebrew Bible, copied and marked by scribes called Masoretes, about 600–1000 CE
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun in the 200s BCE
ancient Jewish manuscripts found near Qumran from 1947 onward, many from about 250 BCE to 70 CE
the careful comparison of manuscripts to find the most likely original wording

look.title: Three Witnesses, One Verse
look.text: King James Version (1611), from the Masoretic Text: he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel. Dead Sea Scroll 4QDeut j: according to the number of the sons of God. Most Septuagint copies: according to the number of the angels of God.
look.prompt: Two of the three witnesses agree in meaning. What else would a text critic want to know before choosing a reading?

check.q: What does the Dead Sea Scroll 4QDeut j read in Deuteronomy 32:8?
check.why: The Qumran scroll reads sons of God (bene elohim) where the Masoretic Text reads sons of Israel.

check.q: What is the Septuagint?
choices: The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible
A Dead Sea Scroll of Deuteronomy
check.why: The Septuagint is the ancient Greek translation, begun in the 200s BCE.

check.q: In textual criticism, what does the word criticism mean?
check.why: Textual criticism means careful judgment between manuscript readings, not attacking the text.

lessons.title: Why a Scribe Might Change a Word
lessons.mainIdea: Text critics reason that a scribe was more likely to change sons of God to sons of Israel than the reverse, while some defend the Masoretic reading with the number seventy.
reading: When manuscripts disagree, text critics ask which reading best explains how the others came about. One rule of thumb is that the harder reading is often older. A scribe copying a puzzling phrase might smooth it into something easier. Scribes rarely made an easy phrase harder.

Apply that rule to Deuteronomy 32:8. Sons of God, meaning heavenly beings over the nations, could trouble later readers worried about other gods. Sons of Israel is easier to accept. So most text critics judge that a scribe changed God to Israel, not the other way around. Heiser made this case in his 2001 article and in The Unseen Realm (2015).

The Masoretic reading has defenders and its own tradition of explanation. Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 count seventy people of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt. Jewish tradition counts seventy nations in Genesis 10. The medieval Jewish commentator Rashi linked the two, so that the nations match the number of Israel's household. That reading gives sons of Israel a clear meaning.

Heiser answered that the number seventy fits the sons of God reading just as well, since Ugarit spoke of seventy sons of El's wife Athirat. Here a student can see an argument at work. Both sides use the same number, and each explains it in a different way.

words.d: a text-critical rule of thumb: the more difficult wording is often the older one, since scribes tended to smooth
a person who copied texts by hand
a Jewish commentator in France (1040–1105) whose notes on the Bible and Talmud are still widely read

lessons.title: Monotheism: Two Accounts
lessons.mainIdea: Mark S. Smith describes Israel's monotheism as developing over time, while Heiser argued the Hebrew Bible consistently presents one unique God among other heavenly beings.
reading: Mark S. Smith is a leading scholar of Ugarit and the Hebrew Bible. In The Early History of God (1990) and The Origins of Biblical Monotheism (2001), he argues that Israel's religion developed over centuries. In his view, early Israel shared much with its Canaanite neighbors. Over time, the worship of Yahweh absorbed features of other gods and pushed others aside. Clear statements of *monotheism* appear, he argues, in texts from around the time of the Babylonian exile, such as Isaiah 40–55.

Heiser disagreed with parts of this story. He argued that the canonical Hebrew Bible, as it stands, presents one consistent picture: one species-unique God with a council of lesser elohim. He wrote about this in a 2008 article in the Bulletin for Biblical Research. There he asked whether terms like monotheism, polytheism, monolatry and henotheism describe the texts well.

Both scholars read verses such as Isaiah 45:5, where God says there is no God beside him. Smith and many others read such verses as denying that other gods exist. Heiser read them as statements of incomparability: no other being is like Yahweh. He pointed out that the same books still mention other heavenly beings, which, he argued, shows the writers were not denying their existence.

This debate is ongoing. It involves how to date biblical texts, how to read Ugarit, and what ancient people meant by a god. Smith works mainly with a historical account of how ideas changed. Heiser worked mainly with the final form of the canon. A student can learn from both by noticing which question each is asking.

words.d: belief in one God; scholars differ on when and how it appears in ancient Israel
the quality of having no equal; Heiser read many 'no other god' verses this way
the collection of books a community accepts as Scripture
the period when many people of Judah were taken to Babylon, from 586 BCE until about 538 BCE

look.title: One Verse, Two Readings
look.text: Isaiah 45:5, King James Version (1611): I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me. Reading 1 (Smith and many others): the verse denies that any other gods exist. Reading 2 (Heiser): the verse says no other being compares to the LORD, while other heavenly beings still exist.
look.prompt: What evidence from elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible would you need to decide between these readings?

check.q: Which book did Mark S. Smith publish in 1990?
check.why: Mark S. Smith published The Early History of God in 1990.

check.q: How did Heiser read verses like Isaiah 45:5?
choices: As later additions to be removed
As statements that no other being compares to the LORD
As proof that Baal is the LORD
check.why: Heiser read these as incomparability statements, not denials that other heavenly beings exist.

check.q: What is the main difference in approach between Smith and Heiser?
choices: Smith traces how ideas changed over time; Heiser worked mainly with the final form of the canon
Smith reads only Greek; Heiser reads only Hebrew
Smith rejects Ugarit; Heiser rejects the Psalms
check.why: Smith gives a historical account of development; Heiser read the canon as it now stands.

lessons.title: Elyon and Yahweh in Deuteronomy 32
lessons.mainIdea: Some scholars read Deuteronomy 32:8–9 as the high god Elyon giving Israel to Yahweh, while Heiser argued Elyon and Yahweh are the same God in the poem.
reading: Deuteronomy 32:8 names the Most High, in Hebrew *Elyon*, as the one who divides the nations. Verse 9 says that the LORD's portion is his people, and Jacob his inheritance. The question is whether these two verses speak of one God or two.

Some scholars, including Mark S. Smith, have read the verses against the Ugaritic picture of El and his sons. In that reading, Elyon is the high god. Yahweh is one of his sons, who receives Israel as his share, just as other sons receive other nations. If so, the verse preserves an older stage of belief in which Yahweh and El were distinct.

Heiser argued against this in his dissertation and articles. He pointed out that the same poem calls Yahweh the father who created and formed Israel (verse 6). He also noted that it says Yahweh alone led Israel with no foreign god (verse 12). And elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, Elyon and Yahweh are used as names of one God. For Heiser, the poem shows one God who places the nations under others and keeps Israel for himself.

Both readings take the Hebrew seriously and both use Ugarit. They differ in how they weigh the rest of the poem and the rest of the canon. This is a good example of why reading a whole passage, not one verse, matters.

words.d: a Hebrew title meaning Most High, used for God in Deuteronomy 32:8 and many Psalms
in Deuteronomy 32:9, the people who belong to the LORD as his own share
a share given to someone; in Deuteronomy 32:9 Israel is the LORD's portion

look.title: The LORD's Portion
look.text: For the LORD'S portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.
look.prompt: Read this verse right after verse 8. Does it sound like the same God, or a second figure? Which words helped you decide?

check.q: What does the Hebrew title Elyon mean?
check.why: Elyon means Most High. Deuteronomy 32:8 names Elyon as the one who divides the nations.

check.q: In the reading Heiser opposed, who is Yahweh in Deuteronomy 32:8–9?
choices: One of Elyon's sons who receives Israel as his share
check.why: Some scholars read Yahweh as a son of Elyon given Israel, like the sons of El at Ugarit.

check.q: Which verse did Heiser cite to show that Yahweh alone led Israel with no foreign god?
check.why: Deuteronomy 32:12 says the LORD alone led Israel. Heiser used it with verse 6 to argue one God is meant.

lessons.title: Two Powers in Heaven
lessons.mainIdea: Alan Segal showed that early rabbis condemned a belief in two powers in heaven; Heiser argued its roots lay in Hebrew Bible texts about a second Yahweh figure.
reading: In 1977 Alan Segal published Two Powers in Heaven: Early Rabbinic Reports about Christianity and Gnosticism. Segal studied passages in rabbinic literature that warn against people who say there are two powers in heaven. The rabbis treated this as a serious error. Segal argued that the idea was older than the warnings. He also argued that it grew from how some Jews read certain biblical passages, and that the rabbis came to reject it as heresy.

Which passages? One is Daniel 7:9–14. There the Ancient of Days sits on a throne, and one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and receives everlasting rule. Another is the Angel of the LORD, who in some stories speaks as God, as in Exodus 3. In Exodus 23:20–21 God says his name is in the angel he sends.

Heiser built on Segal. In his dissertation (2004) and in The Unseen Realm (2015), he argued that the Hebrew Bible itself contains a pattern of two Yahweh figures, one unseen and one visible. He argued that early Christians read Jesus into that pattern. Heiser suggested that this Christian reading helps explain why the rabbis came to treat two powers as heresy.

Jewish tradition reads these passages differently. The Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4, declares that the LORD is one, and rabbinic Judaism understands God's oneness as excluding any second divine person. The Angel of the LORD is read as a created messenger speaking for God. Scholars such as Daniel Boyarin have also discussed the two-powers debate, each with their own conclusions.

words.d: a belief the early rabbis condemned: that a second divine figure shared heaven's rule
a figure in the Hebrew Bible who sometimes speaks as God; readers explain him differently
the declaration in Deuteronomy 6:4 that the LORD is one, central to Jewish prayer
a belief a religious community officially rejects as seriously wrong

look.title: Daniel's Throne Scene
look.text: Daniel 7:9–14, described in our own words: thrones are set up and the Ancient of Days takes his seat, with white clothing and hair like wool. Then one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven. He is brought before the Ancient of Days and given rule that will never end.
look.prompt: How might a rabbinic reader, a Christian reader and Heiser each explain the one like a son of man?

check.q: What did Alan Segal study in Two Powers in Heaven (1977)?
choices: Rabbinic warnings against belief in two powers in heaven
check.why: Segal studied rabbinic reports condemning the two-powers belief and traced its roots.

check.q: What does the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) declare?
check.why: The Shema declares that the LORD is one, which rabbinic Judaism reads as excluding a second divine person.

check.q: In which passage does God say his name is in the angel he sends?
check.why: Exodus 23:20–21 says God's name is in the angel. Heiser used it for his two-Yahweh-figures argument.

lessons.title: Heiser and 1 Enoch
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser treated 1 Enoch as important background for the New Testament, not as Scripture, and scholars differ on how much weight it should carry.
reading: Jude 14–15 cites a prophecy of Enoch, the seventh from Adam. The words closely match 1 Enoch 1:9. Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 mention angels who sinned and are held in chains for judgment. 2 Peter 2:4 uses a Greek verb built on the word *Tartarus*, a place of punishment in Greek thought. These details fit the story of the Watchers in 1 Enoch 6–16.

Heiser argued that the New Testament writers knew 1 Enoch well. He did not claim that 1 Enoch belongs in the Bible. He called it important background: a book many Jews read in the centuries before Jesus, which shaped how they understood Genesis 6. He wrote A Companion to the Book of Enoch (2020) to help readers study it.

1 Enoch has a different status in different traditions. It is canonical only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches. Jewish tradition did not include it in the Hebrew Bible, and most Christian churches left it out too. Many copies of parts of it were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls in Aramaic, which shows it was read widely around 200 BCE to 70 CE.

Critics have raised questions about Heiser's use of 1 Enoch. Some worry that it can lead readers to read too much of Enoch's story into Genesis. Others note that Genesis 6:1–4 is very brief and that its own details should come first. Heiser's supporters reply that he always drew the line between background and Scripture. Students can check how he did so in each case.

words.d: in Greek thought, a deep place of punishment; 2 Peter 2:4 uses a verb built on this word
accepted as part of Scripture by a particular community
the texts and ideas that surrounded a writer and help explain what they wrote

look.title: Jude Cites Enoch

look.prompt: Jude's words closely match 1 Enoch 1:9. Does quoting a book mean treating it as Scripture? What are other possibilities?

check.q: Which New Testament book cites a prophecy of Enoch that matches 1 Enoch 1:9?
check.why: Jude 14–15 cites Enoch's prophecy, which closely matches 1 Enoch 1:9.

check.q: How did Heiser treat 1 Enoch?
choices: As important background, not as Scripture
check.why: Heiser called 1 Enoch important background for the New Testament, not canonical Scripture.

choices: The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches
check.why: 1 Enoch is canonical only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches.

lessons.title: The Sethite View
lessons.mainIdea: The Sethite view reads the sons of God in Genesis 6 as the godly line of Seth, and it has long defenders, though Heiser argued the phrase names heavenly beings.
reading: Genesis 6:2 says the sons of God saw that the daughters of humans were beautiful and took wives from among them. Who were the sons of God? The *Sethite view* answers: descendants of Seth, Adam's third son, who worshiped God. The daughters of humans, in this view, came from the line of Cain. The sin was the godly line marrying outside the faith.

This view has a long history. Julius Africanus, a Christian writer of the early 200s CE, held it. Augustine discussed it in The City of God (early 400s CE). Many Protestant commentators have held it since. Its defenders point to Genesis 4–5, where the lines of Cain and Seth are set side by side. They also cite Matthew 22:30, where Jesus says that in the resurrection people do not marry but are like the angels in heaven.

Heiser argued against the Sethite view in The Unseen Realm (2015) and Reversing Hermon (2017). He pointed out that the phrase sons of God in Job 1:6, 2:1 and 38:7 clearly names heavenly beings. He noted that Genesis never calls the line of Seth the sons of God. And he said Matthew 22:30 speaks of angels in heaven, not those who left heaven, as Jude 6 describes.

A third reading, found in some Jewish sources and some modern scholars, sees the sons of God as powerful rulers or kings. Each reading has passages it explains well and passages it struggles with. A fair student lists both for each.

words.d: the reading of Genesis 6:2 that takes the sons of God as the godly descendants of Seth
the third son of Adam and Eve in Genesis 4:25
a North African bishop and theologian (354–430 CE) who wrote The City of God

look.title: Weighing Three Readings
look.text: Genesis 6:2, sons of God took wives. Reading A (Heiser, following 1 Enoch): heavenly beings. Reading B (Sethite): Seth's godly descendants. Reading C (some Jewish sources and modern scholars): powerful rulers. Evidence to weigh: Job 1:6; Genesis 4–5; Matthew 22:30; Jude 6.
look.prompt: Pick one reading. Which piece of evidence helps it most, and which is hardest for it to explain?

check.q: In the Sethite view, who are the sons of God in Genesis 6:2?
check.why: The Sethite view reads the sons of God as the godly line of Seth, Adam's third son.

check.q: Which verse do Sethite defenders cite about angels and marriage?
check.why: Matthew 22:30 says people in the resurrection do not marry but are like angels in heaven.

check.q: Which argument did Heiser make against the Sethite view?
choices: Genesis never calls the line of Seth the sons of God, while Job uses the phrase for heavenly beings
1 Enoch is part of the Protestant Bible
check.why: Heiser noted the phrase names heavenly beings in Job, and Genesis never applies it to Seth's line.

lessons.title: The Three Rebellions
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser organized the early chapters of Genesis around three rebellions in the unseen realm, a framework some readers find helpful and others think goes beyond the texts.
reading: In The Unseen Realm (2015), Heiser proposed that Genesis 3–11 tells of three rebellions. The first is in Eden, where the serpent, in Hebrew *nachash*, deceives the first humans (Genesis 3). The second is the sons of God crossing into the human world in Genesis 6:1–4. The third follows Babel (Genesis 11). There, Heiser argued, God set the nations under members of his council (Deuteronomy 32:8), and those beings later ruled unjustly (Psalm 82).

Heiser used this framework to explain many later passages. He linked the gods of the nations to the idea that each nation had a heavenly ruler, as in Daniel 10. He also connected the framework to his reading of what the New Testament says about Jesus and the powers. For many readers, the framework gives a clear map of passages that had seemed scattered.

Other readers raise questions. Genesis never uses the word rebellion for Babel's heavenly side, and Deuteronomy 32:8 does not say the sons of God rebelled then. Psalm 82 does not say when their wrongdoing began. Critics say the framework joins texts from different books and times into a tighter system than any one of them states.

Christian tradition has usually spoken of one fall in heaven and one fall of humanity in Eden. Heiser's framework adds two more events. Whether a reader finds it convincing depends on how they weigh links between books. It also depends on how much they allow later texts, such as 1 Enoch, to shape the reading of earlier ones.

words.d: the Hebrew word for the serpent in Genesis 3; Heiser argued it can also suggest a shining one
a big-picture way of organizing many texts so they fit together
the city in Genesis 11 where people built a tower and God scattered the nations

look.title: Where the Three Rebellions Appear
rows: The sons of God, Genesis chapter
Babel and the nations, Genesis chapter
look.cite: Heiser, The Unseen Realm (2015), described in our own words; Genesis
look.prompt: The three events span nine chapters. What might a critic say about linking them as one pattern?

check.q: What is the Hebrew word for the serpent in Genesis 3?
check.why: Nachash is the Hebrew word for the serpent in Eden.

check.q: Which three events make up Heiser's three rebellions?
choices: Creation, the Exodus and the exile
Eden, the sons of God in Genesis 6, and the nations after Babel
check.why: Heiser pointed to Eden, Genesis 6:1–4 and the nations after Babel.

check.q: What is a main criticism of the three-rebellions framework?
choices: It joins texts into a tighter system than any one of them states
It is based on Ugaritic alphabet studies
check.why: Critics say the framework links texts from different books into more of a system than they state.

lessons.title: Jewish Readings
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish tradition includes more than one reading of these passages: earlier texts like 1 Enoch saw angels in Genesis 6, while rabbinic sources mostly read powerful men.
reading: It is easy to speak of the Jewish view as if there were only one. There is not. Books such as 1 Enoch and Jubilees, written by Jews in the centuries before the rabbis, read the sons of God in Genesis 6 as angels. The Jewish writer Philo of Alexandria, in the first century CE, also discussed them as angels in his treatise On the Giants.

Later rabbinic tradition mostly took another path. The *Targum* Onkelos, an Aramaic translation, renders sons of God in Genesis 6:2 as sons of the great ones, meaning nobles or rulers. The *midrash* Genesis Rabbah reads it as sons of judges. Rashi, in the 1000s, explained them as sons of princes and judges. In this line of reading, the sin of Genesis 6 was the abuse of power by the mighty.

Jewish readers also have their own explanations of the council passages. Genesis Rabbah, on Genesis 1:26, has God consulting the angels before creating humans. So the idea of a heavenly court is not foreign to Jewish tradition. What rabbinic Judaism rejects is any reading that would give a second being a share in God's divine rule.

Heiser drew heavily on Second Temple Jewish texts such as 1 Enoch and the Dead Sea Scrolls. His work shows how one strand of ancient Jewish reading shaped early Christians. A fair study notes that Jewish tradition as a whole developed many readings, and that today's Jewish communities read these passages in their own ways.

words.d: an ancient Aramaic translation and explanation of books of the Hebrew Bible
rabbinic interpretation of Scripture, and the collections that contain it
a Jewish philosopher in Egypt in the first century CE who wrote on the Bible in Greek

look.title: Genesis 6:2 Across Jewish History
look.text: 1 Enoch (oldest parts about 300–200 BCE): angels, called Watchers. Philo, On the Giants (first century CE): angels. Targum Onkelos (early centuries CE): sons of the great ones. Genesis Rabbah (about 400s CE): sons of judges. Rashi (1000s CE): sons of princes and judges.
look.prompt: What change do you see over time? What might explain why readings shifted?

check.q: How does Targum Onkelos render sons of God in Genesis 6:2?
check.why: Targum Onkelos, an Aramaic translation, reads sons of the great ones, meaning nobles or rulers.

check.q: Which Jewish text read the sons of God in Genesis 6 as angels?
check.why: 1 Enoch, an early Jewish text, tells of angels called Watchers coming down.

check.q: What is a midrash?
choices: A Dead Sea Scroll of Deuteronomy
check.why: Midrash is rabbinic interpretation of Scripture, such as Genesis Rabbah.

lessons.title: Claim, Evidence, Counter-Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: To weigh any reading fairly, name its claim, list its evidence, and state the strongest evidence against it.
reading: Every interpretation makes a *claim*. Heiser's claim about Psalm 82 is that the gods are divine beings in God's council. A claim should be stated plainly, in one sentence, so that it can be tested.

Next comes *evidence*. For Heiser's claim, the evidence includes the phrase council of El, the Ugaritic parallels, and the sentence you will die like humans in verse 7. It also includes the link to Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Dead Sea Scroll reading. Good evidence is specific: a verse, a word, a manuscript.

Then comes *counter-evidence*, the facts that are hardest for the claim. For Heiser's reading, a reader might point to John 10:34–35, where Jesus refers to those to whom the word of God came. Some take that to mean humans. For the human-judges reading, the hardest facts are the council setting and the phrase die like humans. Stating the counter-evidence against your own view is not weakness. It is what makes a conclusion trustworthy.

Scholars add one more step: they ask how confident the evidence allows them to be. Some claims, like the Qumran reading of Deuteronomy 32:8, have wide support. Others, like the three rebellions, are debated. Saying which is which is part of reading an argument honestly.

words.d: a statement an argument sets out to prove
specific facts, such as verses, words or manuscripts, that support a claim
the facts that are hardest for a claim to explain

look.title: Fill In the Chart
look.text: Claim: In Psalm 82 the gods are human judges. Evidence: judges act in God's name; Jesus quotes the psalm about those to whom the word of God came (John 10:34–35). Counter-evidence: ?
look.prompt: Fill in the counter-evidence line using what you learned about Psalm 82 and Ugarit.

check.q: What is counter-evidence?
choices: The facts that are hardest for a claim to explain
A second claim on a new topic
check.why: Counter-evidence is what a claim must still explain or answer.

check.q: Which is counter-evidence against the human-judges reading of Psalm 82?
choices: The sentence that they will die like humans
check.why: Telling humans they will die like humans is hard to explain. Heiser used this against the human reading.

check.q: Which of these has wide scholarly support, not just debate?
choices: The claim that Ugarit was Israelite
check.why: Most text critics prefer the Qumran reading of Deuteronomy 32:8. The framework is debated.

lessons.title: Reading a Scholar Fairly
lessons.mainIdea: Reading fairly means stating a scholar's view in its strongest form, checking the sources, and separating wide agreement from open debate.
reading: Heiser has many readers who admire him and some who disagree with him strongly. A fair student takes neither side too quickly. The first step is to state his view in a way he would recognize. A weak summary is easy to knock down. Some teachers call the fair approach *steelmanning*: building the strongest version of a view before judging it.

The second step is checking sources. When Heiser says a Dead Sea Scroll reads sons of God, a student can look up 4QDeut j in published editions and modern translations. When he cites a Ugaritic phrase, the student can find it in a scholarly translation of the Ugaritic texts. The same goes for his critics. A claim is only as good as the source behind it.

The third step is sorting. From this unit, a student could list what is widely shared: the divine council imagery, the Ugaritic parallels, the Qumran reading of Deuteronomy 32:8. Then a second list of what is debated: how monotheism developed, the three rebellions, how much weight to give 1 Enoch, the Sethite view. Keeping those lists separate prevents a common mistake, which is treating a debated claim as settled or a settled one as mere opinion.

Finally, a fair reader stays respectful of everyone in the conversation. Heiser, Smith, Segal, Jewish commentators and Christian ones all read closely and carefully. Readers of any faith or none can study their arguments and reach their own conclusions.

words.d: stating an opposing view in its strongest form before responding to it
an original text, such as a Bible passage, a scroll or a Ugaritic tablet
a book or article about primary sources, such as a commentary or a scholar's study

look.title: Sort the Claims
look.text: 1. The Hebrew Bible contains council scenes such as 1 Kings 22. 2. Ugaritic texts speak of an assembly of the sons of El. 3. Genesis 3, 6 and 11 describe three rebellions in the unseen realm. 4. 1 Enoch should shape how Genesis 6 is read. 5. A Dead Sea Scroll reads sons of God in Deuteronomy 32:8.
look.prompt: Put each claim in one of two lists: widely shared or still debated. Give a reason for one of your choices.

check.q: What is steelmanning?
choices: Stating an opposing view in its strongest form before responding
Summarizing a view in its weakest form
check.why: Steelmanning builds the strongest version of a view before judging it.

check.q: Which of these is a primary source?
choices: Mullen's The Assembly of the Gods
A modern commentary on the Psalms
check.why: A scroll is an original text. The books about it are secondary sources.

check.q: What common mistake does sorting claims into shared and debated help prevent?
choices: Treating a debated claim as settled, or a settled one as mere opinion
check.why: Keeping the lists separate helps a reader judge each claim at the right level of confidence.

review.q: Which idea was widely discussed by scholars before Heiser wrote The Unseen Realm?
choices: The divine council in the Hebrew Bible
The Sethite view as Heiser's own invention
review.why: Cross (1973), Mullen (1980) and Smith (1990) all discussed the divine council before 2015.

review.q: Where does the reading sons of God in Deuteronomy 32:8 come from?
choices: A Dead Sea Scroll, supported by the Septuagint's angels of God
review.why: 4QDeut j reads sons of God, and most Septuagint copies read angels of God.

review.q: What did Alan Segal show in Two Powers in Heaven?
choices: That the rabbis condemned belief in two powers, an idea with older roots
That 1 Enoch is in every Bible
review.why: Segal studied rabbinic warnings against the two-powers belief and argued the idea was older.

review.q: Which scholar argues that Israel's monotheism developed over centuries from a Canaanite setting?
review.why: Mark S. Smith, in The Early History of God and later works, argues for this development.

review.q: Which early Christian writer held the Sethite view of Genesis 6?
review.why: Julius Africanus, in the early 200s CE, read the sons of God as Seth's descendants.

review.q: How did most rabbinic sources read the sons of God in Genesis 6?
choices: As powerful men, such as nobles or judges
As the seventy sons of Athirat
review.why: Targum Onkelos, Genesis Rabbah and Rashi read them as great ones, judges or princes.

review.q: Which New Testament verse uses a verb built on the word Tartarus?
review.why: 2 Peter 2:4 uses a verb built on Tartarus for the angels who sinned.

review.q: In the claim-evidence-counter-evidence method, what should a fair reader do with their own view?
choices: List only the evidence that supports it
State the strongest counter-evidence against it
Avoid stating it in one sentence
review.why: Stating the counter-evidence against your own view makes a conclusion trustworthy.
